Comparing Beane to the "Gold Standard" GM's (and The Rest of the League)
stories.summary:
Comparing Beane’s results, relative to the gold standard GM's: Veach, Roseman, and Snead?



	 



	I wanted to bring a more analytical approach to this post, versus a lot of others that are based on "feel", or rely heavily on cherry picking (or dumpster diving) to make a GM seem better or worse, than the overall reality.



	 



	When comparing Brandon Beane with Les Snead, Howie Roseman and Brett Veach, draft position matters. A GM drafting at No. 30 did not pass on the players selected before him.



	 



	I used two draft-position-adjusted models:



	1. All rounds: Measures overall drafting, depth and late-round value.



	2. Rounds 1–3 only: Focuses on the valuable picks expected to produce core players.



	The first model counts every advantage, including the “extra pennies in the cup holder” found when a late pick slightly beats expectations. The second removes most of that noise and asks which GM did the most with meaningful draft capital.



	 



	The main result: Beane finishes first in both



	⠀



	How the models work



	I used Draft Value Added, or DVA. It compares each player’s production with what teams normally get from that exact draft position.



	Simply put:



	• A good player taken late gets more credit than the same player taken early.



	• An early-round miss hurts more than a late-round miss.



	• GMs are not punished because their teams regularly draft near the bottom of each round.



	The classes included are:



	• Snead and Roseman: 2017–2024



	• Beane and Veach: 2018–2024, since neither ran the 2017 draft



	The 2025 and 2026 classes are excluded because those players have not had enough time to be fairly judged.



	DVA measures production compared with draft position. It does not fully measure positional value, playoff impact or whether the drafting team retained the player for that production.



	⠀



	Natural draft positions at No. 20 or earlier



	By “natural draft position,” I mean the team’s original first-round spot based on its record, before any trades.



	 



	• Les Snead, Rams since 2012: 8 times



	No. 2, 16, 13, 10, 15, 5, 6 and 19



	 



	• Howie Roseman, Eagles since 2010: 7 times



	No. 15, 4, 20, 13, 12, 6 and 19



	 



	• Brandon Beane, Bills since 2017: 1 time



	No. 9



	 



	• Brett Veach, Chiefs since 2017: 1 time



	No. 9



	 



	This does not prove Beane is a better drafter. It shows why comparing each GM’s best players without accounting for draft position can be misleading.



	 



	The better question is: Who got the most from the picks actually available to them?



	⠀



	 



	***MODEL 1: ALL ROUNDS***



	 



	DVA per graded pick



	1. Beane: +6.3



	2. Snead: +1.6



	3. Veach: -0.2



	4. Roseman: -3.0



	⠀



	Total DVA produced



	1. Beane: +296.2



	2. Snead: +114.8



	3. Veach: -8.4



	4. Roseman: -162.6



	⠀



	Picks that beat draft-slot expectations



	1. Beane: 62%



	2. Veach: 51%



	3. Snead: 48%



	4. Roseman: 44%



	A negative DVA does not automatically mean terrible drafting. It means those picks produced less than the model expected from those exact draft positions.



	⠀



	What stands out about each GM



	Brandon Beane



	Beane’s advantage is consistency. Buffalo has repeatedly identified useful players outside the premium rounds, including:



	• Taron Johnson, No. 121



	• Khalil Shakir, No. 148



	• Wyatt Teller, No. 166



	• Christian Benford, No. 185



	• Dane Jackson, No. 239



	 



	(Wyatt Teller context. Beane identified him in Round 5, but Buffalo traded him before his best seasons. DVA credits the selection even though Cleveland captured most of the value.  That shows the difference between identifying a player and actually keeping the player long enough to benefit.)



	⠀



	Brett Veach



	Veach has been less consistent, but several of his hits became major parts of championship teams:



	• Trent McDuffie, No. 21



	• Creed Humphrey, No. 63



	• L’Jarius Sneed, No. 138



	• Trey Smith, No. 226



	• Isiah Pacheco, No. 251



	Veach has arguably concentrated more of his value into home runs with direct championship impact.



	(Patrick Mahomes is not included because Kansas City drafted him before Veach officially became GM.)



	⠀



	Les Snead



	Snead has also found substantial middle- and late-round value:



	• Cooper Kupp, No. 69



	• Kyren Williams, No. 164



	• Puka Nacua, No. 177



	• Jordan Fuller, No. 199



	• Quentin Lake, No. 211



	Snead is probably the closest comparison to Beane as a middle- and late-round drafter.



	Snead also combined those hits with aggressive trades for established players. That helped build a championship roster, but it goes beyond drafting alone.



	⠀



	Howie Roseman



	Roseman shows why “best GM” and “best drafter” are not necessarily the same thing.



	His notable draft hits include:



	• Cooper DeJean, No. 40



	• Dallas Goedert, No. 49



	• Jalen Hurts, No. 53



	• Josh Sweat, No. 130



	• Jordan Mailata, No. 233



	Roseman’s pick-by-pick results are less consistent than Beane’s. His larger strengths are accumulating picks, working the board, investing in premium positions and quickly correcting mistakes.



	⠀



	***MODEL 2: ROUNDS 1–3 ONLY***



	 



	The full model counts every pick, but not every win has the same impact.



	A late-round player slightly beating expectations is useful. It normally matters less than turning a first-, second- or third-round pick into a core starter.



	This model removes most of the "coupon clipping found value" effect and counts only Rounds 1–3.



	⠀



	DVA per premium pick



	1. Beane: +5.0



	2. Roseman: +3.4



	3. Snead: +2.6



	4. Veach: -6.2



	⠀



	Total premium-pick DVA



	1. Beane: +106.0



	2. Roseman: +79.1



	3. Snead: +54.5



	4. Veach: -130.7



	⠀



	Premium picks that beat expectations



	1. Beane: 71%



	2. Snead: 67%



	3. Roseman: 61%



	4. Veach: 52%



	⠀



	Premium-pick summary



	• Beane: 21 graded picks, with 15 beating expectations



	• Roseman: 23 graded picks, with 14 beating expectations



	• Snead: 21 graded picks, with 14 beating expectations



	• Veach: 21 graded picks, with 11 beating expectations



	 



	This is the most important result.



	 



	Beane’s lead is not being created only by Day 3 players slightly beating low expectations. He still ranks first when the comparison is limited to Rounds 1–3.



	Roseman improves significantly in the premium model. Snead remains efficient in both. Veach’s overall draft record is helped substantially by major Day 3 hits.



	⠀



	Home runs and championship impact



	DVA still does not perfectly measure elite talent or championship impact.



	Veach has a strong case for producing the most concentrated group of championship contributors. Creed Humphrey, Trey Smith, Isiah Pacheco, L’Jarius Sneed, Trent McDuffie and Nick Bolton all became important pieces of championship teams.



	 



	Snead found stars such as Cooper Kupp and Puka Nacua while using other assets to help build a Super Bowl roster.



	 



	Roseman found a franchise quarterback in Round 2 and several core players at premium positions.



	 



	Beane has Josh Allen, the biggest possible home run. The fair criticism is that Buffalo has not found enough elite non-quarterback difference-makers after Allen.



	⠀



	My takeaway



	The data does not support the claim that Beane is a bad drafter.  In fact, it shows the opposite, from an analytical standpoint!



	 



	He finishes first in overall:



	-DVA per pick



	-Total DVA and percentage of picks beating expectations



	-He also finishes first in all three categories when the comparison is limited to Rounds 1–3



	 



	His advantage is not just Day 3 players slightly beating low expectations.



	The better criticism is that Buffalo has not found enough elite non-quarterback difference-makers.



	Beane has consistently found starters, role players and depth.



	 



	Veach, Snead and Roseman have been less consistent, but each has a case for producing more concentrated championship-level talent.



	 



	So both things can be true:



	Beane has extracted the most value from the picks available to him.



	Buffalo still has not turned enough of that value into elite talent capable of changing postseason games.



	 



	 



	Sources



	Overall GM rankings and explanation of DVA:



	https://sticktothemodel.com/draft/gm



	 



	Beane’s pick-by-pick results:



	https://sticktothemodel.com/draft/gm/brandon-beane



	 



	Veach’s pick-by-pick results:



	https://sticktothemodel.com/draft/gm/brett-veach



	 



	Snead’s pick-by-pick results:



	https://sticktothemodel.com/draft/gm/les-snead



	 



	Roseman’s pick-by-pick results:



	https://sticktothemodel.com/draft/gm/howie-roseman

stories.title: T McGee’s Halloween NHL Mock Draft | Scandinavian Delight
stories.summary:
Excitement!



DBTB –



Let me be honest:  I am getting excited about this Class.  There you go.  Now you know.  Will the Sabres have a 1st round pick this year?  Will they wind up with more than one?  Who can say?  Nobody at this time last year thought they would be selecting at #4 overall AND #20, but that’s exactly what happened.  So strange things can occur.  Thus, I will continue to follow these young prospects, really more for my own entertainment, but also for you, DBTB, in the event you have a hankering for some junior hockey or are, like Casey Kasem before you, keeping your feet on the ground while reaching for (future) stars! 



Why, McGee?  What makes you like this year’s class?  Let’s get into it.  First off, I think drafts are largely valued by how many first-line centers might be in the class.  Some of the great drafts – 1979, 1984, 2003, 2015 – have been anchored by superstar centers.  Lemieux, McDavid, Eichel, Aho, Getzlaf, Staal, Bergeron, etc.  This Draft class has some potential high-end #1 centers – Milan Sundstrom, Yevgeni Yakunin, Alexis Joseph, Jonah Neuenschwander, Brock England, Jaakko Wycisk, Carter Meyer, Max Calce.  Some of those, maybe all of them, will not pan out as 1Cs, but there’s a chance several of them could.  That would automatically make this Draft memorable.  Another thing those elite drafts had were top end D-Men.  2003 had Shea Weber and Ryan Suter.  2015 had Zach Werenski.  1979 had Ray Bourque and Kevin Lowe.  This draft has Landon Dupont, right now the consensus #1 overall.  Assuming he lives up to the hype, that’s another point in this Draft’s favor.  Lastly, an assortment of high-powered offensive forwards is a must.  Marner, Rantanen, and Connor came out of the 2015 class.  1984 had Gary Roberts, Brett Hull, and Luc Robitaille.  Back in 2003, they had Pavelski, Corey Perry, Thomas Vanek, Jeff Carter, Parise, and Brett Burns (some of you will know that Burns was drafted as a right wing and played win in the NHL when he broke in before they switched him to defense).  This year’s Draft has 3 Russian forwards: Privalov, Skvortsov, and Pustovoy.  It also has Dima Zhilkin, Tomas Selic, Tim Kazda, and Noah Davidson, among others.  All of them could be super-productive top-line players.   



Now, just to be clear, I’m not saying this is guaranteed to be an all-time Draft.  Just that it has the potential to receive such lofty status.  What’s the hold up, you might ask.



At the moment, we’re still in the infancy of the 2027 Draft year.  Some teams over in Europe or Russia have played 8-10 games, but most are below that.  Here in North America, at the time of this typing the CHL is only a couple games into the season, while the USHL has barely gotten underway and the NCAA will kick off this weekend. 



What about the Sabres, you might say.  Isn’t this a Sabres’ site?  Indeed it is.  The BFLO prospect pool hasn’t played much as of yet, as they are heavily into the NCAA which just got underway.  But some standouts are worth mentioning here.  First off, Jake Richard.  The big-shot forward and AHL rookie has looked really good, contributing 2P in 2 games in the pre-season, and added his first goal in Game 1 of the Amerks’ season.  If he continues to put up points, he will have exceeded a lot of expectations.  In Russia, Prokhor Poltapov has 5P in 11 games on the best team in the league, loaded with former NHLers and former draft picks.   In the Quebec League, Samuel Meloche has been one of the league’s best goaltenders, notching a 2.54 GAA and a .913 SV% between the pipes for Saint John.  More to come of course, but the Sabres pipeline still looks impressive.



For the last time this season, I’ll be using the odds from the sportsbook at the Wynn in Las Vegas, and then running them through the Tankathon simulator to get my drafting order.  When we hit the November Mock Draft, we’ll have some actual standings that will determine the order of selection.  Until then, we’ll stick with this!

Sabres Analysis



1#20: BUFFALO: Luca Santala, 6’3 C/RW, OHL:  



This Finnish kid might be a little too similar to Ilya Morozov, but you can never have too many good two-way centermen.  Santala has great size (6’2 195#), and the best word I’ve seen used to describe him is ‘complete’.  He can play up and down the line-up, has a mature defensive game even at his young age, and is dangerous on specials teams.  Versatility is another way to describe his game.  A natural goal-scorer, Santala seems like he’s always ready to shoot.  Stick on the ice, feet positioned correctly, has a quick, deadly release whether off the pass, pouncing on a loose puck, or carrying it himself.  Accurate, hard wrister which he can get off without a moment’s hesitation.  Superb hands.  Really good on tips, deflections, and quick shots in tight.  Strong on his skates.  Can power through stick checks with or without the puck.  Real nose for the puck.  Is a clever playmaker, sees the ice well, especially in transition.  



While he seems to be more of a shooter than a passer, he makes the right decisions with the puck in the offensive zone and creates time and space with his puck handling to open things up for teammates.  Slippery with or without the puck, has the courage to try a lot of different things and often gets away with them.  Strong skater, but still room to improve.  His straight-line speed is good, and he’s elusive with the puck, but his motor sometimes seems to downshift for stretches in-game.  That needs to improve, but it’s not that unusual for a number of Finnish prospects…for example, Anton Lundell used to have that same criticism of his game around the same age.  



Defensively, Santala has really good instincts.  On the puck, he uses a quick stick and his smarts to close out his check and take the puck away.  In space, he can flash some high-level defensive recognition, but like his motor, sometimes that wanes for periods during the game.  Could stand to play a little deeper in his own end, especially when playing center.  Santala has the ability to be a valuable #2 center, or he can play wing and serve as a one-timer threat on the PP.  Was great in the Hlinka tournament with 6P in 5 games for the Finns.  Came over to North American this year, intending to play for Dale Hunter and the London Knights, but was traded almost immediately to the Kitchener Rangers (due to some rules re: import players in CHL) where he’ll get plenty of opportunities to play.  Could be a bigger, stronger Mikel Granlund when all is said and done.  And there’s something to be said for that. 













2#20: BUFFALO: Ben Nystrom, 6’3 C/W, SWE:  



A monster on skates, Nystrom is an often-overlooked player out of Sweden.  At 6’3 200#, he’s got plenty of size, and the flexibility to play center or wing.  He’s also a physical presence who has shown a surprising aptitude for scoring.  Make no mistake, Nystrom is a big body who loves to mix it up.  A puck possession beast, knows how to use his size to shield the puck from opponents while looking for open teammates.  Wins more than his share of board battles.  Fearless in going to the corners or behind the net to dig out pucks.  That fearlessness comes from using his obvious size advantage, including his length, to take on smaller players and just overpower them.  But this kid is not a one-trick pony.  He understands how to use that advantage to improve other parts of his game.  



Surprisingly good hands allow him to handle the puck while protecting it and lets him see the ice well enough to make plays and distribute the puck with some skill.  In particular, he can be dangerous out of the cycle, going low to high or cross-crease to set up teammates when he comes out of the corners with the puck, which he does the majority of the time.  Also owns a quick, heavy and dangerous wrister, that he can get off in close quarters with velocity.  Could use some more variety in his shot arsenal, but he’s not a goal-scorer from distance so that might not be as big of a deal.  Encourages a physical game.  Will run opponents over to recover pucks or blast his check with a heavy hit into the boards.  Also tough to handle around the crease, where he uses his length and power to set up shop and can’t be moved.  



Defensively willing, an eager back-checker.  Loves to separate an opponent from the puck and is a very dangerous forechecker with a great sense of timing to jump a passing lane or just take the body and force a turnover.  Has had a great start in the U20 Swedish league with 6P in 7 games.  Was such a productive player at the Hlinka tournament last Spring, he played the final games on the top line for Team Sweden.  Has a lot of similar qualities to former Sabre prospect Anton Wahlberg, but with more of a physical edge.  Reminds me a bit of long-time NHL’er David Backes. 







3#15: BUFFALO (WASHINGTON/SAN JOSE):  Bogdan Yakushevsky, 6’0 W, OHL:  



With a name like a hardware store owner from Cheektowaga, you might be fooled into thinking you know what kind of player he is.  But it’s very likely he goes higher than this from what I’ve seen.  Let’s hope he slides to BFLO.  This kid is a dogged, relentless forward with a ton of skill.  A dynamic puck handler and playmaker, he’s equal parts scorer and passer which makes him all the more difficult to stop.  A player with a great burst, he can get out of the gates in a flash and explodes down the ice.  Couple that with his handle and he makes a lot happen with the puck on his stick in transition.  Takes unexpected routes to the net.  Agility is very good, allows him to go inside or out with ease and keep defenders off guard.  



An absolute terror in puck pursuit.  Yakushevsky never quits on a puck, even when it is recovered by another team.  He’s fast and physical, even at 6’0 190#.  Will throw some big checks on the forecheck, but he gets inside opponents, ties up their hands, and forces turnovers.  Like Zach Benson, he’s always F1 on the forecheck.  Comes barreling in without a second of hesitation.  If he misses the opponent, he’s instantly after them like a dog on a bone.  His unceasing motor has him going all out seemingly every shift.  Puck pursuit is top notch.  But what makes him especially valuable is his ability to score.  Armed with a rocket shot, elusiveness, and the ability to create time and space for himself, he’s a threat all over the ice.  Deceptive with his shot, he can disguise it with a series of fakes or use a defender to hide his intentions until he rips a shot.  And that shot is precise and heavy, enabling him to score from the top of the circles on down, often beating goalies clean from distance.  



A true competitor, the kind the Sabres have been drafting of late (Benson, Helenius, Morozov, Ziemer, etc), he fits a need and a pattern for Jerry Forton and his team.  Unexpectedly came over to North America this year, signing with the Windsor Spitfires and taking the CHL by storm with 5P in 4 games already.  If I squint hard enough, I can see a Sam Bennett-type of player here.   







3#20: BUFFALO: Grady Pichette, 6’4 RHD, WHL:  



Another quality name, the Sabres have made a living the last few years drafting big, rangy defensemen who can skate and play both ways.  In this scenario, they find another one at the back-end of the 3rd round.  Pichette meets all the criteria.  Skating is smooth and effortless for a kid of his size.  He can explode up ice or use his tight turns to recover when transition goes bad and he needs to protect his own end.  When forced to defend he uses that smooth skating and his length to close off opponents and eliminate their options.  Difficult to get behind him.  Meticulous in his play, he has a knack for doing the little things – angling forwards off to the perimeter, maintaining stick-on-puck, tying guys up around the net – that will help him as he continues to evolve.  Really came on in the back-half of last season, when things seemed to click for him.  



Truly more of a puck transporter than an offensive or shut-down guy, he has some upside on both ends.  Needs to play more physical in his D-zone.  Pairing that up with his skating and length would make him an effective shut-down guy not unlike a bigger Ryan Johnson.  Getting more confidence on the offensive side of the puck should allow him to trigger transition more efficiently and then trail the play or even lead the rush more often and create chances from the back-end.  Has all the physical tools the Sabres look for, now he just needs some coaching to start building out his game.  



Playing on an improving Lethbridge team should help with that.  He’s their best defender in the early going this year.  Could become a Marcus Pettersson-type of defender, which has a lot of value in the NHL these days.

stories.title: A Few Thoughts about the Raiders Game, in no particular order
stories.summary:
After last week's recap, I've decided I'm going to try something different. I think I've gotten so caught up in the overall trends of this team that I'm not really allowing myself to enjoy individual games anymore. Every bad play reminds me of something from three weeks ago, and every good play comes with a "yeah, but will that work in the playoffs?" So, for my own sanity, and probably yours too, I'm going to try to look at each game in a vacuum. I'll save my bigger-picture concerns for the final thought each week and hopefully find a little more enjoyment in watching football again.  With that being said, I missed the opening Bills drive (Thanks YouTubeTV), so apparently I also missed Brady burning two timeouts before the game even really got going. Maybe that was for the best.



	 



	1 - Josh - I thought Josh played a pretty good game overall, even if it wasn't the type of performance we've become accustomed to seeing from him. The Raiders were getting consistent pressure and Josh wasn't running nearly as much as we've seen in previous games. Instead, he seemed more willing to take what was available underneath, especially early with Cook and Davis. I liked seeing that because I think it's something he needs to continue doing to make defenses respect the shorter throws.  There were still some classic Josh moments. The broken play where he found Palmer for 34 yards was ridiculous, and the pump fake where he managed to completely fool two defenders was almost comical. Then there's the little chest flip pass to Coleman for the touchdown. I have to remind myself not to take these plays for granted where he makes things look so effortless. I also appreciated seeing him put the ball at Shakir's chest on the WR screen touchdown instead of at his knees, which allowed Shakir to immediately take off. It's a small thing, but something I've complained about before. Overall, Josh didn't need to be Superman today, and that's a good thing.



	 



	2 - Cook - I was really interested in seeing how Cook would respond after the fumbles last week, and I thought he had a really good game. You could clearly see him making an effort to secure the ball with both hands, almost to the point where it looked like he was thinking about it on every carry. But it didn't seem to take away from his running ability. He was making good cuts, finding holes, and continuing to show why he's such an important part of this offense. I also liked seeing him more involved in the passing game, especially on the drive where we went back ahead in the fourth quarter.  The one thing that drove me crazy was him running out of bounds with 2:40 left. What are you doing?! We could have taken that clock all the way down to the two-minute warning. I know he's trying to make a play, but situational awareness matters. Fortunately, we picked up the first down on the next play and it didn't cost us. Outside of that, this was exactly the type of bounce-back performance I wanted to see from him.



	 



	3 - Coleman - I might have been more impressed with Coleman today than I've been in a while. The 22-yard catch against zone coverage was nice, but it was the contested catches that really stood out to me. The comeback route where he went up and fought for the ball was excellent. That's the type of play we've been waiting to consistently see from him. He also made another great catch late in the fourth quarter when we needed to keep the drive moving.  And of course, there's the touchdown on the ridiculous little flip pass from Josh. I don't know if Coleman has suddenly turned a corner or if this was just a good matchup for him, but he looked much more engaged and physical today. I've been pretty critical of him, so I'm more than happy to give him credit when he earns it. Hopefully this is something he can build on, because we desperately need another receiver who can make contested catches and give Josh a reliable target.



	 



	4 - What do you want me to do
	To do for you to see you through?
	For this is all a dream we dreamed
	One afternoon, long ago



	 



	5 - Benford - I thought Benford had a really good game, especially considering he was being asked to cover Bowers for much of it. Bowers is one of the best tight ends in football and Benford was doing a great job taking him away. I believe Bowers didn't even record his first catch until there were about five minutes left in the third quarter. That's impressive. Which is why I was completely baffled when we stopped having Benford cover him. Suddenly Bowers is making big plays and the Raiders are moving right down the field. Then Benford gets back on him and immediately breaks up a pass. I don't understand why we would get away from something that was clearly working. Benford deserves a lot of credit because he showed exactly why he's one of the most important players on this defense. When he's able to take away the opposing team's best receiving threat, it makes everyone else's job easier.



	 



	6 - Ty Johnson - I really liked seeing Ty involved early in this game. Between him and Kincaid, it felt like we were making a conscious effort to get some different players involved in the passing game. Ty is one of those guys who doesn't need a ton of touches to make an impact, but every time he gets the ball, I feel like there's an opportunity for something good to happen. I know Cook is going to get the majority of the work, and rightfully so, but I think Ty brings a different element to the offense. He's reliable as a receiver, has good speed, and can be a weapon in space. I would love to see him continue getting a handful of opportunities each game, especially when defenses are focusing so much attention on Cook. Sometimes the easiest way to help Josh is to give him another simple option who can turn a short pass into something more.



	 



	7 - Walker - What a monster game from Walker. I feel like every time I looked up, he was either pushing someone into the backfield or blowing up a running play. The tackle where he basically piggybacked the running back into the ground was ridiculous. He was also getting the better of Linderbaum on multiple plays, which is no small accomplishment. I know defensive tackles don't always get the attention that edge rushers do, but Walker was impossible to miss today. We need guys who can consistently win their individual matchups and disrupt plays without having to bring extra pressure. Walker did exactly that. Great game from him.



	 



	8 - The Defense - This was a strange defensive performance because there were stretches where I thought we looked really good, and others where the Raiders seemed to be able to move the ball whenever they wanted. The opening drive was frustrating with multiple third-down conversions and Bernard getting absolutely steamrolled on the touchdown. Then later, Bernard gets dragged for another few yards by a tight end. I'm not sure what's going on there, but those are plays he has to make.  I really do thing it's Shaq time coming out of the bye week.  On the positive side, IGB had two big pass breakups, including the third-and-goal stop. Bishop made a couple of really nice plays, including a great hit to break up a pass. Dorian Williams came away with the interception, even if Cousins basically threw it right at him. Gaines had a great play near the goal line, Groot batted down a pass late, and Kilgore made an excellent read to break up the third-down throw on the Raiders' final meaningful possession.  But the fourth quarter was frustrating. We had a 10-point lead and then completely stopped generating pressure. Bowers started getting open, the Raiders moved right down the field, and suddenly the game was tied. Even after we went back ahead, we gave up the deep shot to Tucker, who ran right past Kilgore and IGB. That's a play you simply can't allow in that situation. Fortunately, Shakir recovered the onside kick and we were able to end it.



	 



	9 - Brady - I'm trying not to let this turn into another rant, but there were some things today that made absolutely no sense to me. First off, how do you burn two timeouts on the opening drive? I missed the drive itself, so maybe there's context I'm missing, but that's a pretty terrible way to start a game.  I did like seeing Josh take the underneath throws, getting Ty involved, and mixing things up on the drive where we retook the lead in the fourth quarter. But then there's the drive where we didn't run the ball a single time. Why?! Cook was running well, the Raiders were getting pressure on Josh, and we completely abandoned the run. We punt, and the Raiders go right down the field and tie the game. Then there's the holding call on Torrence that wiped out the fourth-down touchdown to Kincaid. I thought that was a terrible call, but it was another example of a promising drive being derailed.  Overall, I thought the offense did enough to win, but there were still stretches where we made things much harder than they needed to be.



	 



	10 - Bigger Picture - Okay, so here's where I'm allowing myself to look beyond this particular game. We won, and there were some legitimately encouraging individual performances.  I think Bishop, IGB, Dorian, Shakir, Benford, and Coleman are all coming into form.  Josh was able to win without having to carry the entire offense. Cook bounced back from last week's fumbles. Coleman made some excellent catches. Benford showed he can take away an elite receiving threat. Walker was a monster. Those are all positives.  But I still can't ignore the fact that we blew a 10-point fourth-quarter lead against the Raiders and then almost did it again.  We continue to have stretches where the offense can't get out of its own way and our defense seems incapable of protecting a lead without making things interesting. The penalties (Hawes is becoming an issue with the false starts), situational mistakes, and inability to consistently pressure the quarterback are all things that we've seen before.  I also think it's worth remembering that this game could have gone very differently if we didn't make some of those late plays. Kilgore's breakup, the facemask penalty on the punt return, Bass making the field goal, and Shakir recovering the onside kick all mattered. We made enough plays to win, but it certainly wasn't comfortable. I'm going to stick with my new approach and try not to let those concerns take away from the good things we saw today. Every game doesn't need to be a statement about whether we're going to win the Super Bowl. Sometimes it's okay to just appreciate a win and move on.



	 



	*I'm not giving CJGJ the satisfaction of a thought, but if we made changes at MLB and SS during the bye, I wouldn't be opposed.



	**I see that Adams is going to be out for 6-8 weeks in LA.  Think they'd want Palmer?



	 



	On to the bye week and a stress free Sunday where hopefully the Chiefs, Ravens, and Patriots find a way to lose.  I'm very curious to see what changes Leonhard has in store for this defense and hopefully we get to see Oliver and Moore back 100%.  



	 



	Go Bills!!!!

stories.title: THE ROCKPILE REVIEW - Another Good Game to Build On
stories.summary:
The Bills beat the Raiders in Las Vegas on Sunday. The final was 33-30. Bills’ fans are in another tizzy—the defense gave up 30 points, again!



	 



	Yes, I saw the 30 points, and yes, I’m a homer. What I saw was a W. What I saw was a team getting better.



	 



	I’ll start from where I always start: What matters in October is Ws. What matters in December is Ws and how you’re getting them. In December and January, you need very good defense and an offense good enough to overcome other good defenses. The fact that the Bills defense is not championship caliber right now doesn’t bother me, too much. What I want to see is Ws and improvement. And that’s what the Bills are giving me, so I’m happy, for now.



	 



	Some will say, “What improvement? They gave up 30 points!” My response: Don’t worry about the points, not yet. Look at how they’re playing.



	 



	Look at their rushing defense. They gave a total of 65 yards rushing, 3.3 yards per carry. The Bills are now tied for ninth in the league in yards allowed per carry.



	 



	Look at their pass defense. Yes, sure, they gave up a lot of yards passing, and that needs to come down. But what I was seeing on the field was a defensive backfield continuing to play better. Benford looked like Benford again, staying with Bowers and making every reception difficult. Igbinosun looked like a player, with several pass breakups and solid tackling. Hairston looked better. Alford is making plays.



	 



	We all remember the big plays against the Bills, like the bomb to Tucker for the touchdown that got the Raiders to 30 late in the game. What we don’t remember are the incompletions. Cousins is an accurate passer, but the Bills forced a lot of incompletions, with a combination of pressure from the front four and good cornerback play. Cousins was 23-41 and an interception, for a passer rating of 87. Coming into the game, his passer rating was over 100. Allen had the same 23 completions on 8 fewer throws.



	 



	The fact is that the Raiders couldn’t run against the Bills (they haven’t been able to run against anyone), so they threw the ball a lot. What did they get out of all those throws? Not enough to beat the Bills.



	 



	The defensive line looked good. No sacks, but several pressures and several solid plays across the line. Deone Walker continues to sparkle, and Greg Rousseau was at it again, harassing Cousins and playing tough on the line. Parker’s coming into his own, and Carter is contributing consistently.



	 



	Fans like to bash Terrell Bernard, but he is quietly making plays and holding the defense together. Dorian Williams is developing into a solid defender in the passing game, a role in which he was woefully deficient in previous seasons.



	 



	Safety is the biggest positional weakness, where Bishop continues to underperform and Gardner-Johnson continues to hurt the team with missed tackles and penalties.



	 



	The defense is far from being playoff ready, but it’s heading in the right direction. The bye comes at a good time for them.



	 



	On offense, the most pleasant surprise is Keon Coleman. I’m starting to think that Keon just may have needed his rookie season to get used to it all, and it was our expectations that that were the problem. By that I mean in 2025 we saw from him what we expected to see from him in his rookie season, and now we are seeing what we hoped we’d get last season. He isn’t lighting it up, he isn’t on any defensive coordinator’s game plan, but he’s becoming a dependable playmaker.



	 



	The Bills need DJ Moore on the field, who will attract enough attention to make Coleman and Shakir as dangerous as they can be.



	 



	Josh Allen? He’s spectacular. He’s the reason the Bills are 5-1. However, I’m beginning to wonder if he’s ever really mastered the quarterback position as it’s intended to be played. In particular, other than quick little throws to players in the flat and an occasional sideline throw, Josh doesn’t to seem to make the routine 2.3-second throw to the receiver breaking open somewhere. It’s as though instead of finding an easy completion somewhere, he’s waiting for the scramble drill to begin. I’m convinced he misses routine completions every game, and makes up for some of them later in the play.



	 



	The touchdown pass to Coleman would be the play of a career for almost every other NFL quarterback. For Allen, it was just the play of the week. The only reason there won’t be another one next week is the Bills have a bye.



	 



	What bothered me most about the game was Joe Brady’s bonehead clock management at the end of the game. With 2:32 on the clock, it was second and 9 from the Raiders’ 23, and the Raiders had just used their last time out. Allen threw incomplete to Coleman. 2:27 left. Allen threw to Shakir for three yards, and the clock ran to the two-minute warning. On fourth down, the Bills kicked the field goal to go up ten points, and kicked off with 1:56 left.



	 



	With the clock stopped 2:32 in field goal range, all that mattered was running the clock. The Bills should have run on second down and taken whatever they got. Let the clock run to the two-minute warning. On third down, run again and let the clock run to 1:20. If the Bills had been successful on the two runs (a surprise tush push on second down might have gotten them five or more), they’d have a first down and the game would have been over. But even if they didn’t succeed, they would have had the field goal opportunity but having taken 40 more seconds off the clock.



	 



	Whatever. Everyone, including the coach, is learning.



	 



	Before the season began, and with a daunting front end to the schedule, any rational Bills fan would gladly have settled for the Bills to be 5 and 1 and reasonably healthy at this point in the season. Mission accomplished.



	 



	The fun starts in two weeks. An eleven-week sprint to the playoffs.



	 



	GO BILLS!!!



	 



	The Rockpile Review is written to share the passion we have for the Buffalo Bills. That passion was born in the Rockpile; its parents were everyday people of western New York who translated their dedication to a full day’s hard work and simple pleasures into love for a pro football team.

stories.title: Let’s do an apples-to-apples comparison of Leonhard vs other brand new DC’s
stories.summary:
There are 14 new defensive coordinators in the NFL this year, and 7 of them switched schemes (4-3 to 3-4 or vice versa). So the "new scheme" challenges aren’t unique to us. Half the new DCs in the league are dealing with the exact same thing.



	 



	Leonhard ranks dead last among all 14. Every single other new DC has a better defense right now, including all 6 of the others who switched schemes as well. Nine of the 14 have actually improved their team's ranking from last year, some by 14 to 17 spots. And no defense has fallen off a cliff like we have (we've dropped 24 spots). The next worst drop is 14. We are 10 spots worse than the next worst collapse in the league.



	 



	A recurring theme on the forum right now is that the players need more time, perhaps even a full year, to adjust to the new scheme. These other teams didn’t need that adjustment period. Something more is going on here.



	 



	What I have seen



	 



	- We have repeatedly found ourselves in second/third and short situations with our defensive backs lined up 10 yards off the line of scrimmage. That cushion lets the receiver walk forward 3 yards, turn around, and catch the ball for a first down. That's coaching.



	 



	- On numerous occasions we have seen whole sections of our zone left wide open. That isn't talent either. I mean… it’s not like all of our players are too slow to get there and are trailing behind. That would be talent. It's that nobody even knows they're supposed to be there. That's coaching too. 



	 



	- How many times are we going to have 10 defensive players on the field versus the offense? Do the coaches not know how to count?



	 



	- The stats will show that we ran more man coverage but what it doesn’t show is *when* we ran it. Times when I truly believe we should have (third and long press man, to give our d-line more time to get home), Leonhard instead dropped into a zone and we gave up a large play. 



	 



	- Even our QB pressure rate is worse. It was good for two weeks and then fell off a cliff. We are now 30th in the NFL in pressure %. 



	 



	- I frankly don’t care that our run defense is better. This is not 1982. Why should it matter that our run defense is stout when we are giving up 7 more points per game, and 93.7 more total yards per game, and 128.9 more passing yards, and our defense is generating fewer turnovers? Why should we care that we're stuffing the run when the very next play is a 25-yard pass? 



	 



	I really don’t know what the answer is, because they’re clearly not going to fire him after only six games. But I also don’t really see any evidence that this is going to get drastically better.



	 



	The only option I can realistically think of is to bring in Poyer. he is gone as a player, but I think he did a world of good for Bishop last year and he can probably continue reaping benefits for our defensive backs in general.

stories.title: Sabres come back again, but fall to Canadiens in overtime
stories.summary:
Buffalo erases another two-goal deficit, but Cole Caufield ends the night just 54 seconds into overtime



Boxscore



Score: Buffalo Sabres 3-4 Montreal Canadiens (OT)



Shots: BUF 26-34 MTL



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Norris 2 (Helenius), Quinn (Benson, Samuelsson) SHG, Thompson (Doan, Kulich)



Montreal Canadiens Goals: Bolduc (Suzuki, Slafkovsky) PPG, Caufield (Slafkovsky, Carrier), Texier (Guhle, Carrier), Caufield (Unassisted) OT



Goaltending: Luukkonen 30 saves (.882 SV%), Fowler 23 saves (.885 SV%)



Additional Stats: Buffalo won 36.8% of faceoffs, recorded 18 hits and blocked 17 shots.



Quick Thoughts



First Period – A Good Start Doesn’t Last



For once, the Buffalo Sabres didn’t have to spend the opening minutes digging themselves out of a hole. Josh Norris got Buffalo on the board first, taking a feed from Konsta Helenius and beating Jacob Fowler at 8:21 to give the Sabres a 1-0 lead. Unfortunately, that lead didn’t last long. Montreal answered just over three minutes later when Zachary Bolduc scored on the power play. Cole Caufield followed with another goal at 14:01, and Buffalo suddenly trailed 2-1 after the opening period. It has become a familiar problem for the Sabres this season. Even when they start well, they have struggled to control games and keep opponents from building momentum. Buffalo has shown it can battle back when things aren’t going its way, but it would be nice to see them play with a lead for a change.



Second Period – Jack Quinn to the Rescue



Buffalo got worse early in the second period. Alexandre Texier scored at 7:39, extending Montreal’s lead to 3-1 and putting the Sabres in another two-goal hole. Sound familiar? Just two nights earlier, the Sabres trailed Toronto 4-2 entering the third period before rallying for an overtime win. Apparently, Buffalo tried the same approach against Montreal. Jack Quinn, who was outstanding against Toronto, continued his strong play by scoring a shorthanded goal at 9:52 of the second period. With assists from Zach Benson and Mattias Samuelsson, Quinn brought Buffalo back within one and gave the Sabres some much-needed life. Quinn has quickly become one of Buffalo’s most important offensive contributors. His chemistry with Benson has grown exponentially, and if he keeps this up, he will earn a nice payday. Whether it’s scoring, creating opportunities, or sparking the offense when the team desperately needs it, he keeps finding ways to make an impact. He even made a great backcheck to split up a two-on-one.



Third Period – Here We Go Again



At this point, the Buffalo Sabres might actually prefer playing from behind. For the third straight game, Buffalo needed a comeback, and the Sabres delivered again. This time, Tage Thompson stepped up. At 10:12 of the third period, Thompson finished a play set up by Josh Doan and Jiri Kulich, beating Fowler to tie the game at three. Just like that, another two-goal deficit had disappeared. The Sabres had erased a 3-1 deficit against Montreal on Tuesday, came back from 4-2 down against Toronto on Thursday, and now had fought back from another 3-1 hole against the Canadiens. There is certainly something to be said about a team that refuses to quit. The Sabres have shown impressive resilience early this season, particularly in the third period. When they turn up the offensive pressure and start moving the puck with confidence, they can make life difficult for opponents. But this has become an almost ridiculous trend. Why does Buffalo need to be trailing by two goals before it starts playing its best hockey? The tying goal ensured the Sabres would collect at least one point, but another overtime appearance was waiting.



Overtime – That Didn’t Take Long



After needing overtime against Montreal on Tuesday and Toronto on Thursday, the Sabres were headed back to three-on-three hockey for the third straight game. Unfortunately, this overtime period didn’t last very long. Just 54 seconds into the extra frame, Cole Caufield scored his second goal of the night to give Montreal the 4-3 victory. And just like that, another dramatic Buffalo comeback ended with only one point to show for it. The Sabres have now played beyond regulation four times in their first nine games, including three consecutive overtime or shootout appearances. Buffalo might be getting comfortable playing extra hockey, but there is a difference between fighting back to earn a point and finishing the job.



At The Horn



The Buffalo Sabres are becoming one of the NHL’s most entertaining and frustrating teams to watch. On one hand, this team has shown it can overcome adversity. They don’t seem rattled when trailing by multiple goals, and their offensive players have consistently stepped up when needed. On the other hand, the Sabres are making things unnecessarily difficult for themselves. 



Montreal outshot Buffalo 34-26 and dominated in the faceoff circle, winning 63.2% of the draws. Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen made 30 saves to keep Buffalo within striking distance, but the Sabres once again struggled to play a complete game. 



There are certainly positives to take away from the night. Quinn continued his offensive production, Thompson delivered another important goal, and Norris got Buffalo off to a promising start. But the larger issue remains. The Sabres have now erased two-goal deficits in three straight games. That speaks to their character, but it also raises serious questions about their ability to dictate games rather than constantly reacting to what their opponents do. 



Last season’s successful team found ways to win games without needing dramatic third-period comebacks every night. Buffalo needs to find that same consistency. It’s encouraging to know the Sabres can come back from almost anything. It’s considerably less encouraging that they keep putting themselves in those situations. With a 4-3-2 record in nine games, Buffalo has earned valuable points despite inconsistent performances. But overtime-loser points won’t be enough if the Sabres want to establish themselves as a legitimate contender in the Atlantic Division, and any point earned without Dahlin in the lineup is a good one.

stories.summary:
It’s Déjà Vu All Over Again With Buffalo Back at Bell Centre



Buffalo Sabres (4-3-1) vs Montreal Canadiens (3-3-1)

*knock knock* “Who’s there?” “It’s Déjà Vu”



“Déjà Vu who?”



*knock knock*



What to Watch



1. Do Not Adjust Your TV Sets



The Sabres once again return to the friendly confinds of Bell Centre in Montreal tonight with just four days and one game in Toronto between visits. Unusual scheduling to be sure. This second go-around will finish off the Maple Leaf sandwich with another slice of Montreal French bread.



Last time out, Buffalo stormed back to steal a point in the standings before imploding in the shootout. The Sabres will need a better, more consistent effort in tonight’s matchup with the Habs to come out a winner. No more two-shot periods allowed!



The bad news for Buffalo is that Rasmus Dahlin has been ruled out again for today’s game against the Canadiens, Matthew Fairburn of The Athletic reports.



Head coach Lindy Ruff said Thursday that Dahlin was 50/50 to play Saturday, but the 26-year-old won’t travel with the team to Montreal after all. However, Ruff said Friday that Dahlin is progressing, so it seems possible that he’ll be a candidate to return Wednesday against the Flyers. He remains listed as day-to-day for now.



2. Four Jacks



Jack Quinn tied his career-best performance as a pro in Buffalo’s thrilling 5-4 overtime win over Toronto on Thursday night. The talented winger recorded two goals and two assists for a satisfying four-point night. He also showed some toughness after being confronted by Toronto’s Troy Stecher, handling himself well in a brief fight. To cap off the evening, Quinn set up Owen Power for the overtime winner. What a hand he played for the comeback victory.



Quinn has looked noticeably more confident and effective on the ice this season, as things finally appear to be coming together for the fifth-year Sabre. He is tied for the team lead in both goals and points while averaging 19:20 of ice time per game. Lindy Ruff has repeatedly praised Quinn’s improved speed, growing confidence, and playmaking ability as he enters a crucial contract year. Along with Noah Östlund and Zach Benson, Quinn has helped form what has arguably been Buffalo’s best forward line this season.



Jack has been a major factor so far this year for Buffalo and Thursday’s performance was another encouraging sign of his development. The Sabres will need him to keep this momentum going if the team hopes to build on its recent success. If Quinn continues to play with this level of confidence and consistency, he could be in for a breakout season at just the right time.








Photo Credit: Buffalo Sabres




3. Concussion Grenade



Off to a slow start with just two points in eight games, Josh Norris now finds himself in concussion protocol. At this point, it almost feels like the Sabres’ injury report isn’t complete without him.



Norris collided awkwardly with Oliver Ekman-Larsson during overtime in Toronto and did not return to finish the game. He’s listed as day-to-day and will likely miss at least a game or two. 



UPDATE Norris surprisingly practiced on Friday but the return-to-play process typically spans a minimum of 5 to 6 days (though actual return depends on symptom resolution).



Tyson Kozak can’t step into Norris’s spot as he has been sent home, but Jiri Kulich is the likely option if he’s feeling better. Kulich was recently sent back to Buffalo himself to be evaluated over concerns related to the blood clot he suffered last season. Fortunately, he checked out fine. Jiri has since returned to the team and is listed as a possibility to play tonight.



It’s been a disappointing start to the season for Norris. He opened the year playing top-line minutes but struggled to generate much offense. More recently, he’s been shuffled around the lineup and has seen mostly bottom-six duty. Now he’s dealing with another injury, although this one hopefully won’t keep him out for long. The Sabres are starting to get a little thin at forward.



With Norris, though, you can never be too comfortable. He could get injured opening his mail. 



SECOND UPDATE Norris practiced again this morning and is now a possibility to play tonight. I have to wonder how that’s possible, given the NHL’s mandates with concussions. Either his new evaluation determined he wasn’t actually suffering from a concussion, or something has changed rather quickly.

stories.title: Sabres crunch Leafs in stunning comeback
stories.summary:
Buffalo pulled back another two-goal deficit in the third period for overtime win



Boxscore



Score: Buffalo Sabres 5-4 Toronto Maple Leafs OTShots: BUF 34-30 TOR



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Jack Quinn 3 (Benson, Metsa), Quinn 4 (Östlund, Samuelsson), Gilbert 1 (Quinn, Benson), Samuelsson 2 (Thompson), Power 2 OT (Quinn, Östlund)Toronto Maple Leafs Goals: Matthews 6 (Roslovic), Marchenko 2 PPG (Tavares, Raddysh), Marchenko 3 (Tavares), Marchenko 4 (Sissons, Cowan)



Quick Thoughts



First Period – Pre-season Sabres



What was that first period? Minus Jiri Kulich the entire team except one Jack Quinn seemed to be absent and anything the Leafs got came from Buffalo errors. 




Jack Quinn is the beneficiary of a Toronto turnover after Zach Benson pressured Blankenburg, 1-1 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/xKuELj0Cl0— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 15, 2026




Oh, and if Ukko Pekka Luukkonen has heard the BUF-NYR-WPG triumvirate trade chatter, he certainly didn’t show it. 



Win a damned faceoff. The Leafs led the period 13-7 at the dot and led to a lot of their puck possession.



Remember that whole thing about the Leafs having a plodding defense and that the Sabres should go up the ice vertically against them? Yeah they didn’t really, and the one time they did they scored. 



The Sabres jumped on the Leafs to start, leading 7-2 on shots, but the period ended 15-8 to Toronto. 



The Leafs got lucky with the the refs (hmmm) when they got an undeserving power play to close out the period after their own player high-sticked his teammate. The Leafs fifth-ranked power play ended the period 1 of 2 with a dozen second left in the man advantage. 




Sam Carrick gets a two-minute penalty for having OEL high stick his own teammate pic.twitter.com/PdvV1cdkjn— Crossing Swords ⚔️ (@CrossSwordsPod) October 15, 2026




Second Period – Drought-era Sabres



The Sabres killed of the overlapping power play before Quinn continued his Leaf ownage, scoring his ninth goal in 15 games against Toronto, displaying his patience before McCabe bit and the Sabres forward blasted home over Bobrovsky’s shoulder. 



He almost had a hattie a few minutes later when he waltzed through a static D but Bob refused to be embarrassed again. 




Jack Quinn's 2nd goal of the game, 2-2 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/zdINNj5aRq— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Olen Zellweger decided not only was he going to replace Bowen Byram in the Sabres lineup, but he was going to take a further step and fill Rasmus Dahlin’s sizeable skates. He’s been very visible the last few games and was good again tonight. 



A full session of turnover-filled hockey in the neutral zone then ensued. As the Sabres then got lulled to sleep, Tavares won a board battle in the middle of the period, fed Marchenko and he beat UPL glove side for his second of the game to make it 3-2. 



Quinn hit the post and was active throughout the period again, and when Tage Thompson drew a penalty, Quinn even dropped the gloves against faux hard man Stecher. While he didn’t land a punch, he did wrestle his man to the ice and both drew five for fighting which alas hurt the Sabres more with their in-form top scorer taken off the ice. 



Remember when Knies was traded to the Blue Jackets on the eve of the season and then promptly scored twice against the Sabres on debut? Well the piece that went the other way was Marchenko and then with three minutes left Doan lost him in the blue paint he promptly got his hattrick to make it 4-2. 



With just under two to play Rielly went off for hooking, but Benson took an immature penalty holding on to Sissons’s stick. But unlike that night when the Habs were not punished for that, Benson took a penalty and the power play was wasted. 



Once again the Sabres were going to a third period having spotted their opponent a two-goal lead, despite having outshot the Leafs 13-11 in the period. 



Third Period – Division-winning Sabres



The Sabres have eight third period goals and it has been their best period by far. This one started with the same verve too with Buffalo humming around Bob’s net. 



Paul tripped Josh Norris into Tavares, sending the Leafs forward down the tunnel to the dressing room. 



Tonight though, while Quinn was feeling it, who from the Sabres would step up and get a goal to add some pressure on the home side? Last season it was the defense, and once again tonight it was the dmen again. 



Well, Quinn found Dennis Gilbert at the blue line halfway through the period and the dman fired home over Bob’s pad to make it 4-3. That gave Quinn a very well-deserved Gordie Howe hattrick. Congrats to Buffalo boy and the much-loved Gibby for his first Sabres goal!




Dennis Gilbert gets on the board to make it 4-3 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/M9CbWYHlaX— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Toronto were rocking on their heels and just two minutes later, Mattias Samuelsson joined the rush, took a feed from Tage and roofed a shot over Bob to make it 4-4 and the Scotiabank Arena was hushed. At that point the Sabres were outshooting the Leafs 10-1!




Mattias Samuelsson gets involved and ties the game, 4-4 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/xcVa9T0p9Y— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Toronto belatedly woke up after that, but the rest of regulation time elapsed with little drama, 4-4 and advantage Sabres 11-4 for the period on shots. 



Overtime – He’s Got The Power!



Unlike the OT in Quebec two nights ago when the Sabres barely had a sniff of the puck for five minutes, this one was more end-to-end. 



Benson had the puck on a three-on-one and then whiffed on his pass. Then Norris got clattered in the Leafs defensive zone and Power wisely held on to the puck to allow the forward to hobble off the ice. They went straight up the guy after that with Östlund feeding up Power who then fired off a howitzer to beat Bobrovsky for another OT winner!




Owen Power overtime winner, 5-4 #LetsGoBuffalo #Leafs pic.twitter.com/luzb3aqI1C— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 16, 2026




Make that three straight goals scored by defensemen tonight when the forwards minus Quinn were all sputtering. 



At The Horn



The Sabres simply cannot keep spotting teams leads going into the third period and assuming they can just reel them back in, especially against offensively endowed teams like the Leafs and and even more so when they are still without captain Rasmus Dahlin. 



Luukkonen wasn’t bad tonight, but as he has so often this season, he saved shots he shouldn’t have, and was beaten by shots he should have saved, ending the night on a deficit of -1.03 once again in the Goals Saved Above Average.

What to Watch



1. Zellweger shining in Dahlin’s absence



Olen Zellweger already had big shoes to fill when he was acquired from Anaheim this offseason, and when Sabres captain Rasmus Dahlin went down with an injury in Monday’s win over the Panthers, it forced the 23-year-old into an even bigger role.



Fortunately for Buffalo, he’s certainly looked the part so far.



Zellweger had two goals and finished with a career-high 25:49 of ice time in Tuesday’s shootout loss in Montreal, and led Sabres skaters in shots on goal for the second consecutive game. With Dahlin out again against the Maple Leafs, another standout performance from Zellweger could go a long way toward securing two points in a divisional matchup.



2. Luukkonen finding his game?



Sabres coach Lindy Ruff kept it suffice on Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen’s performance following Tuesday’s game: “Our goalie got us a point.”



Luukkonen stopped 35-of-38 shots against the Canadiens, including a crucial late save with 3 seconds remaining in regulation that secured the Sabres a point. He also finished with a positive goals saved above expected for the second consecutive game, according to Hockeystats.com, following a strong relief appearance against Florida. Despite an abnormally poor showing in the shootout, it seemed like the Finn was finally beginning to get into a rhythm in the crease.



The Sabres will look to Luukkonen again to start on Thursday, but he faces a bogey team in the Maple Leafs. The 27-year-old is 0-5-2 in eight appearances against Toronto in his career.



3. Early elation to frustration



The Sabres were a remarkable 36-6-2 when scoring first last season, a conversion rate that played a major factor in sending the franchise back to the playoffs, but it’s been tough sledding in that category to start this campaign.



Buffalo is 1-2-1 this season when tallying the first goal, a worrying trend albeit one with a small sample size. On top of that, in all four games the Sabres have scored first, they have failed to get the next goal and been outscored 7-3 in the second period.



Should the Sabres score first for the fifth time this season against Toronto, following up on that early momentum would be a welcome sight.



Injury Notes



In addition to being without Dahlin on Thursday, the Sabres will also be down Tyson Kozak, who is dealing with an upper-body injury. Ruff said Wednesday that goalie Alex Lyon suffered a setback in his recovery from a shoulder injury, meaning he’ll be off the ice for a few days after returning to practice last week.



Toronto will be without defenseman Chris Tanev, who is week-to-week with an upper-body injury suffered in the Maple Leafs’ win over Colorado on Sunday.

Sabres escape Montreal with a point, lose 4-3 in shootout
stories.summary:
Score: Buffalo Sabres 3, Montreal Canadiens 4 (SO)



Shots: Buffalo 17, Montreal 38



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Zellweger (1) (Samuelsson, Malenstyn); Norris (1) (Gilbert, Malenstyn); Zellweger (2) (Benson, Samuelsson)



Montreal Canadiens Goals: Lane Hutson (1) (Slafkovský, Caufield); Caufield (3) (Slafkovský, N. Suzuki); Anderson (2) (Huston, Bolduc)



SO Goals



Sabres: Thompson



Montreal: Caufield; Texier; Bolduc



Summary



The Buffalo Sabres (3-3-1), facing some adversity without Captain Rasmus Dahlin dressed, dropped Tuesday night’s game to the Montreal Canadiens (3-2-1) by a score of 4-3 in a shootout. Sabres goalie Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen stops 35 of 38 shots in the loss, including a couple big saves at the end to help secure the Sabres a point. 



A Stop and Go First



It was a sluggish start for both sides in the game, as multiple whistles in the first few minutes prevented either team from finding consistent footing. 



This actually ended up to the Sabres benefit early on.



Just over two minutes into the game, defenseman Olen Zellweger, who was thrust into a bigger role with Dahlin out of the lineup, ripped a shot from the point. Thanks to a friendly bounce off the skate of a Canadiens’ defender in front, this otherwise innocuous shot would give the Sabres a nice early 1-0 lead. 



The flurry of stoppages continued even after the Sabres got their early lead, including one where linesman Ryan Daisy was accidentally hit by Jiri Kulich off a faceoff scrum, leading to Daisy having to be helped off the ice. The game continued with just three officials.



The Sabres went without a shot on goal after their goal until a Too Many Men penalty led to a Sabres power play, and while they did not score, they managed four shots on goal within that two minute span and kept the zone pressure for the entirety of the man advantage. Montreal did not manage one clear, as Benson and Ostlund in particular hounded the Montreal penalty kill unit. While none of the shots were incredibly high danger, it was another encouraging sign for the Sabres power play. Notably with Dahlin out, Power was manning the point alone in his stead. 



Still with their 1-0 lead, the Canadiens found themselves with a golden opportunity. Josh Norris made an ill-advised pass that led to a two-on-zero rush. With a golden chance, Josh Anderson took a cross ice feed and buried it right into the net of Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen’s glove. It was an amazing save by Luukkonen to keep the Sabres lead intact. 



The lead would not last for much longer though, back to back penalties by Zellweger and Louis Crevier would give Montreal a 5 on 3 power play. While the Sabres did a nice job for the first portion, Lane Hutson would make them pay, tying the game 1-1 on a shot from the point. 



Thankfully for the Sabres, they were able to kill enough of the second penalty to whittle it down to 18 seconds left when Montreal would take a penalty of their own, this time a hold. The ensuing Sabres power play was not as effective as the first one, as they struggled to keep zone pressure. The rest of the period remained uneventful, as the Sabres and Habs entered the first period with the score at 1-1. Montreal did have the shot edge in the period, 11-7. 



Uneventful and Opportunistic



The second period started in a sluggish fashion too, but unlike the first period, this was to the Sabres’ disadvantage. Montreal had a good amount of early pressure, which led to the Krebs-Thompson-Doan line being out there for an extended shift. As they tried to push back on offense, they got caught up ice and couldn’t get back, giving Montreal a 4-on-2 rush, leading to the puck finding the stick of Cole Caufield, who made no mistake, blowing a one-timer by Luukkonen to give them a 2-1 lead just two minutes into the period. 



The Sabres continued in the early part of the second period being unable to sustain anything of note. This was not for lack of chances to drive play though, as they found themselves with two early power plays, one before the Caufield goal, and one a few minutes after. Despite the hope the first one gave, the ensuing three opportunities left a lot to be desired. 



What the power play for the Sabres did accomplish, however, was completely stifling momentum for both teams. After that power play, both teams went about 10 minutes recording one shot each. Montreal would get a power play of their own with five minutes remaining in the period, once again bringing the Sabres a challenge on the penalty kill. 



While the Sabres killed that penalty, they could not escape the period down a goal. With under a minute to go, Ryan McLeod failed to clear the puck from the defensive zone, leading to sustained pressure. Unfortunately for McLeod, the puck found the stick of the most dangerous Canadien, Lane Hutson, who drew the attention of every Sabres defender. Hutson slid the puck over to a completely uncovered Anderson, who made no mistake burying a one-timer top shelf past Luukkonen to give the Canadiens a 3-1 lead going into the third period.



The Sabres mustered just two shots in the period, despite even having two opportunities with the man advantage. The Canadiens, despite a 10 minute stretch where they recorded two shots, ended with 11 in the period. The Sabres on the season have been outscored 13-4 in the second period of games so far this season. 



In his post game press conference, Sabres coach Lindy Ruff said the second period against the Canadiens “may have been one of our worst periods in a long time.”



Live with the bounces



The Sabres must have gotten a message heading into the third because they came out with a different pace than they had the first two periods. Just four minutes into the period, Norris put in some good work to win a wall battle, skated to the point, and let a shot go that bounced off a defender before going in the net, cutting the lead to 3-2. It was the first goal of the season for Norris, whose struggles have been one of the biggest talking points of the season for the Sabres so far, but he put in some nice work on that shift to get rewarded with the bounce.



The bounces would continue just a few minutes later, with Olen Zellweger benefitting from a bounce once again. Very similar to the first two Sabres goals, Zellweger let a point shot go that deflected off a defender and past Montreal goalie Jacob Fowler again, tying the game at three, just one minute after Norris scored to cut the lead to one. 



Montreal would respond with a flurry of chances following the tying goal, peppering Luukkonen with shots and while none of them were incredibly high danger, he still faced a ton of action with a flurry of shots. 



After that flurry, both teams seemed content to get a point in overtime. The only real chance until the final few seconds of the game was a Sabres 2-on-1 at the end of a shift that led to Fowler making the save on Josh Doan. 



While the game did indeed go to an extra frame, catastrophe almost struck in the twilight of regulation. Montreal had possession with just under 10 seconds left in the period, and a defensive miscue led to Phillip Danault being all alone in front with the puck off a feed from the wall. Danault put a deflection on Luukkonen, who stood firm, making the initial save and an ensuing rebound save to ensure his team would at least gain one point in the standings. 



Overtime Possessed



Montreal completely dominated possession in the overtime period, putting up five shots in the frame to the Sabres zero. No shots, however, did not mean the Sabres went without chances to win it. 



A Josh Doan that was broken up before he could get a shot off, and actually ended the frame on a 30 second power play from a holding penalty on Juraj Slafkovsky. Some questionable antics from Jake Evans, grabbing the sticks of both Benson and Quinn while lying on the puck on the ice helped kill off that penalty. The Sabres got a couple nice looks at the end of the frame but couldn’t get a puck on Fowler. The game would then go to everyone’s favorite party game…



The Shootout



The Canadiens seemingly had something on Luukkonen, as they scored on all three attempts in the shootout and all attacked from the same angle. Both Caufield and Texier skated right to left and beat Luukkonen clean with a wrister, while Bolduc skated the same direction and beat him through the 5-hole on a deke. The Sabres went 5-1 in games that went to a shootout last season, an area that Luukkonen was great in. The Sabres coaching staff will have some work to do figuring out how to help Luukkonen so this doesn’t continue to happen.



Wrap Up



The Sabres, while they of course would have wanted two, have to feel pretty good escaping this game with a point. They were outplayed for a majority of the game and struggled to generate any offense, despite even having five power play opportunities in the game. All three Sabre goals came off point shot deflections, meaning the result could have been much worse, especially considering they were on the wrong end of a back to back without their best player.



While he let in three goals, Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen is the main reason the Sabres escaped even with one point. Stopping 35 of 38 shots on a night where the team in front of him was really struggling to generate offense is exactly what the Sabres needed to see from their goalie. 



Although he finished with negative goals saved above expected, he didn’t have much of a chance on any of the three that went in, and he made plenty of big time saves to keep the Sabres in the game when they were down and to get the game to overtime once it was tied.



With the Sabres down their captain, they needed a few members of their defense corps to step up. Power and Samuelsson were their normal steady self, but the team had to be incredibly encouraged by Olen Zellweger’s performance in this game. Leaving the two goals aside, he logged over 25 minutes of ice time, only trailing Power and Samuelsson among the defensemen, and has potentially found himself in the circle of trust. If Zellweger can be this kind of player for the Sabres, they will miss Bowen Byram less and less as the season goes on. 



What’s Next



The Sabres will travel to Toronto on Thursday for a showdown with the revamped Maple Leafs. It is unknown to this point if Dahlin will be back in the lineup, but he has not yet been ruled out for the game.

stories.summary:
Buffalo Returns to Montreal for First Meeting Since Playoff Elimination



Know Your Opponent



Montreal Canadiens



Record: 2-2-1 | 5 PTS



Last Game: 1-0 shootout victory over Detroit Red Wings



Division Ranking: 6th in Atlantic Division



PP: 32nd, 5.9% (Sabres: 25th, 13.6%)



PK: 21st, 76.2% (Sabres: 30th, 60.0%)



Season Series: First meeting of 2026-27



What to Watch



1. Back to the Scene of the Crime



The Buffalo Sabres return to Montreal tonight for the first time since their season ended in Game 7 of the second round of the Stanley Cup Playoffs. Alex Newhook’s overtime winner sent the Canadiens to the Eastern Conference Final and left Buffalo wondering what could have been. Now, less than five months later, the two Atlantic Division rivals meet again. While the stakes aren’t nearly as high this time around, there should still be some extra motivation for the Sabres. Buffalo enters tonight’s contest coming off a much-needed 5-3 victory over Florida on Monday afternoon. After Dallas shut them out and Utah allowed only one goal, the Sabres finally got their offense going. Montreal has also had an inconsistent start to the season, sitting at 2-2-1 after Saturday’s shootout win over Detroit. The Canadiens have plenty of offensive talent, but have struggled to put together complete performances. With Buffalo playing the second half of a back-to-back, a strong start will be important.



2. No Dahlin, No Problem?



The biggest storyline heading into tonight is Rasmus Dahlin’s absence. The Sabres captain left Monday’s game against Florida with an upper-body injury and did not travel with the team to Montreal. Dahlin is considered day-to-day, but losing him creates a significant problem for Buffalo. He leads the team’s defense, runs the power play, and plays in nearly every serious situation. Owen Power will need to take on a bigger role. Power has been one of Buffalo’s better starters this season, recording seven points in six games. His offensive production has been encouraging, but tonight will also test his ability to handle more defensive responsibility. Mattias Samuelsson will also be relied on heavily, while Dennis Gilbert has been recalled from Rochester after Matt Grzelcyk was placed on injured reserve. Montreal’s top line of Cole Caufield, Nick Suzuki and Juraj Slafkovsky will present a difficult matchup, particularly without Buffalo’s best defenseman.



3. Special Teams Remain a Problem



Buffalo finally got its power play going against Florida, scoring twice on five opportunities. Dahlin and Noah Östlund each converted with the man advantage, giving the Sabres three power-play goals over their last two games. Unfortunately, the penalty kill remains a disaster. The Panthers entered Monday’s contest with one of the league’s worst power plays and still managed to score twice on four opportunities. Buffalo’s penalty killing percentage has fallen to just 60%, ranking near the bottom of the NHL. Montreal hasn’t been much better on the power play, converting just one of its first 17 opportunities this season. Something has to give tonight. The Canadiens have enough talent in Suzuki, Caufield, and Lane Hutson to make Buffalo pay if the Sabres keep allowing cross-ice passes and quality scoring chances. With Dahlin out, the Sabres will also need someone to quarterback the top power-play unit. Power would be the obvious candidate, and it will be interesting to see how Lindy Ruff adjusts.



4. Can the Sabres Find Some Consistency?



Goaltending is another concern. Colten Ellis was pulled Monday after allowing two goals on nine shots, leaving Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen to finish the game. Luukkonen made 13 saves in relief and is expected to get the start tonight. Monday’s win over Florida was encouraging, but the Sabres still have plenty to clean up. Buffalo has alternated between looking like the team that won the Atlantic Division last season and the team that spent more than a decade missing the playoffs. Against Dallas and Utah, the Sabres struggled to generate consistent offensive pressure. Against Florida, they moved their feet, attacked the middle of the ice, and created opportunities around the net. Tage Thompson has been Buffalo’s most consistent offensive threat, with four goals and seven points in six games. The Sabres need their other forwards to continue contributing. Josh Doan and Ryan McLeod both scored their first goals of the season Monday, while Östlund continues to establish himself as an important part of the lineup. The Sabres don’t need their goalie to steal every game, but they do need more dependable performances if they want to compete with the better teams in the Atlantic Division.

Final Thoughts



It’s hard to overstate the importance of a mid-October game, but tonight gives Buffalo a chance to build momentum. The Sabres have a difficult stretch of divisional games ahead, including Thursday’s matchup in Toronto and another meeting with Montreal on Saturday. Getting points against Atlantic Division opponents will be critical if Buffalo hopes to repeat last season’s success. Playing without Dahlin makes things more difficult, but it is also a chance to see whether the Sabres have enough depth to overcome injuries to key players. Buffalo showed against Florida that it can generate offense throughout the lineup. Now it needs to do so consistently while playing a more responsible defensive game. A win tonight would move the Sabres above .500 for the first time since beating Minnesota last week.
